note_002:
**Pre-norm (Llama-style):** normalize the block input BEFORE attention.
    * The un-normalized input is kept aside as the <back:yellow>residual stream</back>.
    * <back:yellow>RMSNorm</back> = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) x learned scale (gamma) (no mean-centering, no bias).
    **Why normalize before attention?**
    * Every block ADDS its attention output back onto the residual stream, so the stream's scale keeps growing with depth (100, 100.5, ...).
    * A large input makes Q x K^T huge: <back:yellow>softmax</back> saturates (outputs near 0 or 1), its gradient goes to ~0 and training becomes unstable (exploding / vanishing gradients).
    * <back:yellow>RMSNorm resets a COPY of the stream to a standard scale, so attention always sees a safe input</back> and its output stays small and stable.
    * <back:yellow>Only the copy is normalized; the residual stream itself stays untouched</back>, so gradients flow straight through the "+" back to the early blocks (pre-norm, unlike the original post-norm Transformer: no fragile warm-up needed).
    * RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction of LayerNorm: same stability, cheaper.
part_002: Q K V Projection and RoPE
act_004: Raw K matrix = X x W_K
act_005: Raw Q matrix = X x W_Q
note_003:
**Linear Projection (Matrix Multiplication):** X x W_Q, X x W_K, X x W_V (toy values below are assumed).
          Q (<back:yellow>Query</back>) = what a token is looking for. K (<back:yellow>Key</back>) = the label it offers.
          V (<back:yellow>Value</back>) = the content it passes on when picked.
          <back:yellow>Q and K decide WHO to listen to; V is WHAT gets taken in.</back>
          **Toy setup (terms used below):**
          |= Term |= Meaning |= Toy (head 1 shown) |= Llama 3 8B |
          | d_model | length of one token's vector | 4 | 4096 |
          | n_heads | parallel attention heads, each a separate self-attention (Q, K, V\nfrom the same tokens) with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V; their Z are concatenated back to d_model | 2 (head 1 worked out; head 2 is drawn, not computed) | 32 |
          | d_k = d_head = d_model / n_heads | length of one Q, K or V row, per head | 4 / 2 = 2 (V rows too: d_v = d_k) | 4096 / 32 = 128 |
act_007: Final Q_cat = Raw Q_cat x R_position 0
act_008: Final K_cat = Raw K_cat x R_position 0
act_009: Final Q_on = Raw Q_on x R_position 1

note_004:
Right now, the Raw Q and Raw K matrices only contain semantic information—they
          have no concept of sequence order yet. This is the exact moment <back:yellow>RoPE</back>
          (Rotary Position Embedding) steps in to finish generating them.
          <back:yellow>RoPE rotates only Q and K (never V).</back>
          Toy rotation here (d_k = 2, so one dim pair): (0, 1) turns 90° per position.
          90°: [a, b] -> [-b, a].  180°: [a, b] -> [-a, -b].
          (Real RoPE rotates every dim pair of the head, each at its own frequency.)
          The final K and V are appended to the <back:yellow>KV cache</back>, so during <back:yellow>Decode</back>
          only the new token's Q, K, V are computed.
act_012: Raw score cat = [q_cat x k_cat, q_cat x k_on, q_cat x k_desk]
act_013: Raw score on = [q_on x k_cat, q_on x k_on, q_on x k_desk]
act_014: Raw score desk = [q_desk x k_cat, q_desk x k_on, q_desk x k_desk]
note_005:
**Purpose:** score how relevant each token's Key is to this token's Query
        ("how much should token i look at token j?"). Dot product q x k: multiply
        element by element, then add up (sums in the Raw score boxes above).
        <back:yellow>Large = same direction (key matches the query), near 0 = unrelated.</back>
        The GPU scores all pairs at once, <back:yellow>Q x K^T</back>: [3, 2] x [2, 3] = a 3 × 3 grid (row i, column j),
        each cell = 2 multiply-adds (d_k = 2). Raw scores, not weights yet:
        [4.0, 3.0, -1.0]  <- Raw score cat
        [3.0, 1.0, 0.0]  <- Raw score on
        [2.0, 4.0, -2.0]  <- Raw score desk
        "cat" scores highest with itself. "on" aligns most with "cat".
        "desk" aligns most with "on", and also with "cat".
        During <back:yellow>Decode</back> only the last row is computed: the new token's query
        against all cached keys (1 x seq_len scores).
note_006:
To keep the numbers from exploding and blinding the Softmax, the entire grid is divided by <back:yellow>sqrt d_k</back>.
      **Why:** each score is a sum of d_k products, so it grows with d_k; <back:yellow>dividing by sqrt d_k keeps the scale steady.</back>
      Here d_k = 2 (the length of one Q or K row; see the table in the Linear Projection note), so sqrt d_k = sqrt 2 = 1.41.
      The GPU divides every single cell in our matrix by 1.41
      [4.0 / 1.41 = 2.83, 3.0 / 1.41 = 2.12, -1.0 / 1.41 = -0.71]
      [3.0 / 1.41 = 2.12, 1.0 / 1.41 = 0.71, 0.0 / 1.41 = 0.0]
      [2.0 / 1.41 = 1.41, 4.0 / 1.41 = 2.83, -2.0 / 1.41 = -1.41]
note_007:
This is the exact sub-step where the <back:yellow>Causal Mask</back> strikes.
      The system compares the Position ID of the Query (the row)
      against the Position ID of the Key (the column).
      **The Rule:** <back:yellow>If Key Position > Query Position,</back>
      <back:yellow>it is a future token. Replace the score with negative infinity (-∞).</back>
      [2.83, -∞, -∞]
      [2.12, 0.71, -∞]
      [1.41, 2.83, -1.41]
note_008:
When this masked grid is fed into <back:yellow>Softmax</back>,
      the math handles the rows beautifully: Row 0 ("cat"): Because e^-∞ = 0,
      <back:yellow>the future slots get an absolute 0% weight.</back> "cat" is forced to look at itself 100%.
      Row 1 ("on"): The future slot for "desk" gets 0%. The remaining scores (2.12 and 0.71) compete,
      resulting in about 80% cat and 20% on (e^2.12 = 8.33, e^0.71 = 2.03, 8.33 / 10.37 = 0.80).
      Row 2 ("desk"): No values were blocked.
      The scaled scores (1.41, 2.83, -1.41) compete openly, resulting in about
      19% cat, 80% on, and 1% desk (e^1.41 = 4.10, e^2.83 = 16.95, e^-1.41 = 0.24, over their sum 21.29).
note_010:
In this step, the model takes the Attention Map Matrix and multiplies it by the Value Matrix (V).
      <back:yellow>This is where tokens actually exchange information</back>: each token's output Z is a weighted sum of the Value vectors of the tokens it attends to (e.g. "on" = 80% of cat's V + 20% of its own).
      <back:yellow>Context Matrix (Z)</back>=Attention_Map x V
      To see this mathematically, let’s work out head 1 and assume each word's Value vector has d_head = 2 numbers, the same length as Q and K (in real models like Llama 3, d_head is typically 128 numbers per head).
      Let's assign some realistic semantic numbers to our Value vectors:
      V_cat = [2.0, -1.0]
      V_on = [0.0, 3.0]
      V_desk = [5.0, 1.0]
      The GPU multiplies the weights from each row of the Attention Map against the Value columns.
      This is a standard weighted sum performed for each row simultaneously in parallel:
note_014:
Context Matrix (Z) = [
        Slot 0: [2.0, -1.0]    (Context vector for "cat")
        Slot 1: [1.6, -0.2]    (Context vector for "on")
        Slot 2: [0.43, 2.22]  (Context vector for "desk")
      ]
note_015:
**Linear Projection**
    Blends all the parallel attention heads together
    * A learned projection made of trainable parameters (weights)
    * It changes the numbers inside the vectors to blend the context of different heads together.
    * Matrix Multiplication (×)
    1. **Before W_O (The Split Insights):** each of the N heads (2 in the toy, 32 in Llama 3 8B) sees the sentence from its own angle.
      * Head 1 outputs a small vector representing grammatical structure.
      * Head 2 outputs a small vector representing animal traits.
    2. **The Concatenation Step:** the model glues these N separate vectors side-by-side into one ultra-wide vector.
      Right now the values are still raw, isolated pieces of information; they haven't been combined yet.
    3. **The W_O Multiplication (×):** This wide vector is multiplied by the <back:yellow>W_O</back> matrix.
    For "on" (the walkthrough above worked out head 1; head 2 and W_O are assumed values):
    Output = Concat_Z x W_O   ([3, 4] x [4, 4] -> [3, 4], W_O assumed; real: [d_model, d_model])
    Head 1 Z_on = [1.6, -0.2]   Head 2 Z_on = [1.0, 0.5]
    Concatenated = [1.6, -0.2, 1.0, 0.5]   (2 + 2 = d_model = 4)
    Column 0 of W_O = [0.5, -0.2, 0.4, 1.0]
    Output[0] = 1.6x0.5 + (-0.2)x(-0.2) + 1.0x0.4 + 0.5x1.0 = 0.8 + 0.04 + 0.4 + 0.5 = 1.74
    Head 1 gives 0.84 + head 2 gives 0.9: <back:yellow>one number already mixes both heads.</back>
    All 4 columns: attention output for "on" = [1.74, -0.6, 0.17, 0.78]
note_016:
Adds the block input (the <back:yellow>residual stream</back> saved before the pre-attention RMSNorm)
    to the attention output, to prevent data loss
    Toy example for "on" in block 1 (all values from above):
    Block input (embedding_on)  = [-0.688, -0.688, -0.884, 0.732]
    Attention output for "on"   = [1.74, -0.6, 0.17, 0.78]
    Sum (element by element)    = [1.052, -1.288, -0.714, 1.512]
    <back:yellow>Both sides must have the same shape</back> (3 rows, 4 columns each), so W_O brings
    the attention output back to d_model = 4. The sum keeps this shape.
    The original embedding stays inside the sum: <back:yellow>attention only learns the change.</back>
note_017:
**Pre-norm:** normalize BEFORE the FFN. The un-normalized stream
    (after the residual above) is kept aside for the next residual add.
    This is a second, separate <back:yellow>RMSNorm</back> (same formula, its own gamma).
    * Its input is x1 = x0 + attention output, the residual result above.
      That add made the stream's scale bigger again.
    * <back:yellow>The FFN's SwiGLU activation is sensitive to input scale</back>, so x1 is
      normalized (a copy only) before it enters the FFN.
note_018:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>attention moves information between</back>
        tokens; <back:yellow>the FFN processes each token's vector</back>
        on its own (adds non-linearity).
        **How:** expand (gate, up), <back:yellow>SiLU</back> gate filters,
        multiply with up, W_down compresses to d_model.
note_019:
The model takes your token vector
        (e.g., size 4,096) and multiplies it by two separate
        weight matrices to project it into a much larger
        hidden dimension—typically about 2.7 to 3.5 times wider
        (e.g., Llama 3 8B expands 4,096 to 14,336 numbers = 3.5x;
        a small model may use 8/3 = 2.67x).
note_020:
<back:yellow>SiLU(x) = x · sigmoid(x)</back>  (<back:yellow>SwiGLU</back>, as in Llama; some models use GELU instead)
            * Large negative values -> pushed close to 0 (almost OFF)
            * Large positive values -> pass through almost unchanged (ON)
note_021:
**Element-wise multiplication**
        [ 12.5, -0.072, 0.110 ]
        (Activated Vector A / The Filter)
        × [ 5.0,  9.0, -2.0  ]
        (Raw Vector B / The Knowledge Data)
        ---
        = [ 62.5, -0.65, -0.22 ]
        (The Combined Wide Vector)
note_023:
**Stacking by Position Order**
    * A data organization step handled by GPU memory.
    * It changes the physical layout of the vectors,
      stacking them row by row into a matrix.
    * Concatenation / Stacking (No math, just moving data around).
note_024:
Adds the stream saved before the pre-FFN <back:yellow>RMSNorm</back> to the FFN output.
    This sum is the input of the next block.
note_025:
One last <back:yellow>RMSNorm</back> after the final block, before the <back:yellow>LM Head</back>. The stream has accumulated N blocks of additions,
  <back:yellow>so it is rescaled once more to keep the logits at a sane scale</back> (own gamma).
note_026:
matrix slicing operation (or index selection) to grab only the very last vector in the sequence
<back:yellow>(inference only: next-token prediction needs just the last position)</back>.
Training keeps the vectors of ALL positions and computes the loss on each (targets are the inputs shifted by one token).
note_027:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>one score (logit) for every word in the</back>
vocabulary, using the weight matrix <back:yellow>W_vocab</back>
[d_model x vocab_size]. Called "Linear" in the 2017
figure. Real model: 4,096 x 128,000 -> 128,000 logits.
note_029:
**Applied to the logits, before Softmax:**
* **Temperature T:** logits / T. <back:yellow>T < 1 widens the gaps (safer), T > 1 narrows them (more varied)</back>; T = 0 is greedy (<back:yellow>argmax</back>).
|= T |= the |= desk |= water |= cat |= on |= chance of water (5 words, no Top-K) |
| 1 (unchanged) | -0.70 | 1.25 | 3.00 | 0.50 | -0.15 | 76% |
| 0.5 (x 2) | -1.40 | 2.50 | 6.00 | 1.00 | -0.30 | 96% |
| 2 (/ 2) | -0.35 | 0.625 | 1.50 | 0.25 | -0.075 | 48% |
* **Top-K:** keep the K highest logits, the rest become -inf (K = 3: water 3.00, desk 1.25, cat 0.50 stay; on, the cut).
note_030:
**Applied to the probabilities, after Softmax:**
* **Top-P (nucleus):** add up the probabilities from the largest; <back:yellow>keep the smallest set whose total reaches P</back>, drop the rest.
  Unlike a fixed Top-K, the kept set adapts to the model's confidence.
|= P = 0.9 |= water |= desk |= cat |
| Probability | 0.796 | 0.138 | 0.065 |
| Running total | 0.80 | 0.93 (at least 0.9: stop) | |
| Kept? | yes | yes | no |
* **Renormalize:** the kept probabilities no longer sum to 1 (0.7963 + 0.1384 = 0.9347), <back:yellow>so divide each by that total</back>:
  water 0.7963 / 0.9347 = 0.852, desk 0.1384 / 0.9347 = 0.148. Now they sum to 1 again.
* **Sample:** draw a random number in [0, 1): below 0.852 -> water, else desk. T = 0 skips the draw (greedy: always the top word).
  A fixed random seed repeats the same draws; while generating, <back:yellow>this draw is the only random step.</back>

note_032:
Each loop iteration is one <back:yellow>transformer block</back> (N blocks, e.g. 32 in Llama 3 8B),
    each with its own weights (not shared between blocks).
    Weights of ONE block (Llama 3 8B, <back:yellow>d_model</back> = 4096): <back:yellow>learned in training, frozen when generating.</back>
    |= Where |= Weight |= Shape |
    | RMSNorm before attention | gamma | 4096 |
    | Attention | W_Q | 4096 x 4096 |
    |  | W_K | 4096 x 1024 |
    |  | W_V | 4096 x 1024 |
    |  | W_O | 4096 x 4096 |
    | RMSNorm before FFN | gamma | 4096 |
    | FFN (SwiGLU) | W_gate | 4096 x 14336 |
    |  | W_up | 4096 x 14336 |
    |  | W_down | 14336 x 4096 |
    About 218M parameters per block x 32 blocks = 7B (+ embedding and LM Head 1B = 8B in total).

note_043:
"<back:yellow>Llama-style</back>" = Meta's Llama tweaks to the decoder-only Transformer (same core as GPT, GPT-1 2018); now shared by most open models.
    (Meta: Llama 1 Feb 2023, Llama 2 Jul 2023, Llama 3 Apr 2024)
    |= Part |= Original Transformer (2017) / GPT-2 (2019) |= Llama-style |
    | Normalization | LayerNorm; post-norm, pre-norm (GPT-2) | RMSNorm (2019), pre-norm |
    | Position | Absolute position embedding added to input | RoPE (2021): rotates Q and K |
    | FFN, bias | 2 matrices + ReLU / GELU, with biases | SwiGLU (2020): gate, up, down; no biases |
    | K / V heads | Multi-head: as many K/V as Q heads | GQA (2023): fewer K/V heads (Llama 2 70B, 3; not drawn) |

"Llama-style" = RMSNorm (pre-norm), RoPE, SwiGLU, no biases

title_004: Decoder-only Transformer (Llama-style): Architecture at a Glance
note_044:
**Compared with the 2017 figure:**
    * <back:yellow>no cross-attention</back> (no encoder)
    * <back:yellow>pre-norm: RMSNorm comes BEFORE attention and</back>
      the FFN, not "Add & Norm" after them
    * no positional-encoding add at the input:
      <back:yellow>RoPE rotates Q and K inside attention</back>
note_045:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>turn the input text into token IDs (plain numbers).</back>
    **Text -> tokens -> token IDs:**
    1. Text: "cat on desk".
    2. <back:yellow>A tokenizer splits it into tokens</back> (words or word pieces):
       "cat", "on", "desk".
    3. Each token is looked up in the model's fixed vocabulary
       (a table that gives every token it knows a number) and
       replaced by that number: <back:yellow>its token ID, a plain integer.</back>
    **Toy vocabulary** (5 words; the numbers are fixed labels, in
    the same order as the LM Head columns below):
    "the" = 0, "desk" = 1, "water" = 2, "cat" = 3, "on" = 4.
    **Example** with this vocabulary:
    "cat on desk" -> tokens ["cat", "on", "desk"] -> <back:yellow>IDs [3, 4, 1].</back>
    After "water" is picked, the input grows:
    ["cat", "on", "desk", "water"] -> IDs [3, 4, 1, 2].
    (Llama 3: about 128,000 tokens. This diagram shows the words, not the IDs.)
    When generating, the input is the prompt plus every token
    produced so far.
note_046:
**Purpose:** turn each token ID into a vector
    the model can compute with.
    **token ID -> vector:** <back:yellow>the ID is only an index.</back>
    The model keeps a learned table (the embedding matrix)
    with one row per token ID. <back:yellow>The ID selects its row, and</back>
    <back:yellow>that row is the token's vector</back> (a row of d_model numbers).
    **Toy:** ID 3 ("cat") -> row 3 -> [-0.251, 0.901, 0.464, 0.197].
    The row's numbers are learned in training, so similar
    tokens get similar vectors.
    <back:yellow>d_model = the length of this vector</back> (the model's
    "width"): 4 in the toy, 4096 in Llama 3 8B. Every
    <back:yellow>step of every block keeps this width.</back>
note_047:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>keep the numbers at a stable scale</back>
    before attention and before the FFN.
    **Before:** a vector's numbers can be big or small.
    Each block adds its results to every token's vector
    (one row of the matrix), so the numbers
    <back:yellow>keep getting bigger in every block</back>
    (e.g. 100, 100.5, ...). Attention and the FFN would
    get inputs of very different sizes.
    **After:** <back:yellow>the same pattern, rescaled to a steady size.</back>
    **How:** divides each vector by its <back:yellow>root-mean-square</back> (RMS),
    then <back:yellow>multiplies by a learned weight (gamma)</back>.
    **Toy** (4 numbers; "eps", a tiny number like 0.00001 that only avoids dividing by zero, is left out):
    x = [1, 5, 5, 7]
    1. Square each number: [1, 25, 25, 49]
    2. Average them: (1 + 25 + 25 + 49) / 4 = 25
    3. Square root: sqrt(25) = 5. This is the RMS: the average size of the numbers in this vector.
    4. Divide each number by 5: [0.2, 1, 1, 1.4]
    5. Multiply each number by its gamma (one learned number per
       position): with gamma = [0.9, 1.3, 0.7, 1.1] (assumed): [0.18, 1.3, 0.7, 1.54]
    <back:yellow>A vector 100 times bigger, [100, 500, 500, 700], has RMS = 500</back>
    <back:yellow>and gives the same [0.2, 1, 1, 1.4] after step 4: same pattern, size reset.</back>
note_048:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>let each token gather information</back>
    from the tokens before it.
    **Before:** each vector knows only its own token.
    **After:** <back:yellow>it also carries information from the</back>
    tokens before it.
    **Multi-head attention** = <back:yellow>several self-attentions ("heads")</back>
    <back:yellow>running in parallel.</back> Each head has its own Q, K, V:
    it reads the whole vector but makes smaller ones.
    **Toy values** (all assumed).
    The vector of "on", d_model = 4, 2 heads, d_head = d_model (4) / n_heads (2) = 2:
    ""x = [0, -2, -1, 1]""
    **Head 1** (each matrix: 4 rows, 2 columns):
    ""W_Q = [-0.50  0.00]   W_K = [ 0.40 -0.20]   W_V = [0.30  0.60]""
    ""      [-0.25 -0.25]         [-0.50 -0.25]         [0.50 -1.00]""
    ""      [-0.75  0.50]         [-0.50  0.50]         [0.00 -0.50]""
    ""      [-0.25 -1.00]         [ 0.50  1.00]         [1.00  0.50]""
    Head 2 has its own W_Q, W_K, W_V.
    **W_O** (4 rows, 4 columns, one per block):
    ""[ 0.5 -1.0  0.2  0.3]""
    ""[-0.2  0.5  0.5 -0.5]""
    ""[ 0.4  0.6 -0.3 -0.3]""
    ""[ 1.0  1.0  0.5  1.0]""
    **Self-attention steps** (1-6 run inside each head; 7 joins the heads):
    1. <back:yellow>Q, K, V</back>: each token makes a Query (what it looks for), a Key (what it offers), a Value (what it passes on).
       Example (head 1, "on"): Q = x × W_Q, using the values above
       Q[0] = 0×(-0.50) + (-2)×(-0.25) + (-1)×(-0.75) + 1×(-0.25) = 1.0
       Q[1] = 0×0.00 + (-2)×(-0.25) + (-1)×0.50 + 1×(-1.00) = -1.0
       -> Q = [1, -1]. K and V work the same way, with W_K and W_V: K = [2, 1], V = [0, 3].
       <back:yellow>Each output number mixes all 4 input numbers.</back>
    2. <back:yellow>RoPE</back>: rotates Q and K by position, so the attention scores know how far apart two tokens are.
       Example (head 1, "on" is position 1, so one 90° turn: [a, b] -> [-b, a]):
       Q: [1, -1] -> [1, 1]
       K: [2, 1] -> [-1, 2]
       V = [0, 3] stays the same (RoPE never touches V).
       <back:yellow>The turn depends on the position, so Q and K now carry where the token is.</back>
    3. <back:yellow>Attention scores</back> = Q x K^T: how well each Query matches each Key.
       Example (head 1, the row of "on", with Q and K after RoPE): Q_on = [1, 1]
       Q_on · K_cat  = 1×2 + 1×1 = 3
       Q_on · K_on   = 1×(-1) + 1×2 = 1
       Q_on · K_desk = 1×1 + 1×(-1) = 0
       -> scores of "on": [3, 1, 0] (K_cat = [2, 1], K_on = [-1, 2], K_desk = [1, -1])
       <back:yellow>"on" matches "cat" best (3); "desk" is unrelated (0).</back>
    4. <back:yellow>Causal mask</back>: hides future tokens, so none can peek ahead.
       Example (head 1, the row of "on", position 1):
       d_k = d_head = 2 (the length of one Key), so the scores are first divided by
       sqrt(d_k) = sqrt 2 = 1.41: [3, 1, 0] -> [2.12, 0.71, 0.0]
       Why divide: a score is a sum of d_k products, so longer vectors give bigger scores (Llama 3 8B: 128 products).
       <back:yellow>Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the scores at a steady size.</back>
       "desk" is position 2 > 1, a future token -> [2.12, 0.71, -∞]
       <back:yellow>"on" can still see "cat" and itself, but not "desk".</back>
    5. <back:yellow>Softmax</back>: turns each row of scores into weights that sum to 1.
       Example (head 1, the row of "on"): [2.12, 0.71, -∞]
       e^2.12 = 8.33, e^0.71 = 2.03, e^-∞ = 0; sum = 8.33 + 2.03 + 0 = 10.36
       8.33 / 10.36 = 0.80, 2.03 / 10.36 = 0.20, 0 / 10.36 = 0
       -> weights [0.80, 0.20, 0]: "cat" 80%, "on" 20%, "desk" 0% (they sum to 1)
       <back:yellow>The masked slot gets exactly 0%, so "on" cannot peek at "desk".</back>
    6. <back:yellow>Weighted sum of V</back>: blends the Values using those weights.
       Example (head 1, the row of "on"): weights [0.80, 0.20, 0], V_cat = [2, -1], V_on = [0, 3], V_desk = [5, 1]
       Z[0] = 0.80×2 + 0.20×0 + 0×5 = 1.6
       Z[1] = 0.80×(-1) + 0.20×3 + 0×1 = -0.8 + 0.6 = -0.2
       -> Z_on = [1.6, -0.2] (this is head 1's output from the Toy values above)
       <back:yellow>"on" now holds mostly "cat"'s Value (80%) plus a little of its own (20%).</back>
    7. <back:yellow>W_O</back>: mixes the heads' outputs back into one vector.
       Example ("on"): joined = [head 1 Z_on, head 2 Z_on] = [1.6, -0.2, 1.0, 0.5];
       column 0 of W_O = [0.5, -0.2, 0.4, 1.0]
       1.6×0.5 + (-0.2)×(-0.2) + 1.0×0.4 + 0.5×1.0 = 1.74
       (head 1 gives 0.84, head 2 gives 0.9: <back:yellow>one number mixes both heads.</back>)
       All 4 columns: [1.74, -0.6, 0.17, 0.78] = the attention output for "on"
       **Before vs after attention** (the vector of "on", 4 numbers):
       Before: x = [0, -2, -1, 1]  (knows only "on")
       After:  [1.74, -0.6, 0.17, 0.78]  (head 1: 80% of "cat"'s V + 20% of its own V)
       <back:yellow>Same token, same length, but the numbers now carry information from "cat".</back>
note_049:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>add the result of attention (or the FFN)</back>
    <back:yellow>to its own input instead of replacing the input.</back>
    **Before:** two vectors: the input (carried around by
    the <back:yellow>orange arrow</back>) and the result of attention (or the FFN).
    **After:** <back:yellow>one vector = input + result</back>; the old
    information is kept and the new is added.
    <back:yellow>output = input + F(norm(input))</back>, where F is attention
    or the FFN. <back:yellow>So F only has to produce what to add or</back>
    <back:yellow>change, not rebuild the whole vector.</back>
    Used twice per block: after attention and after the FFN.
    Toy ("on", d_model = 4; x and A are the values of the Multi-Head Attention note,
    RMSNorm left out to keep it simple), element by element:
    ""X_on  = [ 0.00, -2.00, -1.00, 1.00]  block input""
    ""A_on  = [ 1.74, -0.60,  0.17, 0.78]  attention output""
    ""X1_on = [ 1.74, -2.60, -0.83, 1.78]  X + A""
    Both have 4 numbers. For all 3 tokens: 3 rows, 4 columns each (W_O brings A back to d_model = 4).
    Attention adds context from earlier tokens; the FFN adds
    what the model knows about each token.
    <back:yellow>The original rows are kept, so each sub-layer only learns what to add.</back>
note_050:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>transform each token's vector on its own</back>
    (no mixing between tokens).
    **Before:** the vector holds the token plus the context
    attention gathered, still unprocessed.
    **After:** the same vector, processed with what the
    model learned. It holds about two-thirds of a
    block's weights; <back:yellow>much of the learned knowledge</back>
    <back:yellow>(facts, patterns) is thought to be stored here.</back>
    <back:yellow>SwiGLU</back> = a gated FFN: a gate decides, per token,
    which features pass. It gives better quality than
    a plain ReLU FFN at the same cost. 4 steps:
    1. <back:yellow>Gate and Up</back>: two parallel projections widen the vector.
    2. <back:yellow>SiLU(gate)</back>: a smooth on/off switch on each gate number.
    3. <back:yellow>SiLU(gate) x up</back>: the gate decides how much of
       each Up number passes (multiplied number by number).
    4. <back:yellow>Down</back>: projects back to d_model.
note_051:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>rescale once more after N blocks</back>
    of additions, before the <back:yellow>LM Head</back>.
note_052:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>one score (logit) for every word</back>
    in the vocabulary.
    Matrix [d_model x vocab_size]. Called "Linear" in the
    2017 figure, the <back:yellow>LM Head</back> or <back:yellow>unembedding</back> here.
    **Toy**: vocab = 5 words; h and W_vocab are assumed values.
    h [1 x 4] x W_vocab [4 x 5] -> logits [1 x 5]
    One logit = h . (one column of W_vocab). For "water":

    |= Vector |= d1 |= d2 |= d3 |= d4 |= Sum |
    | h (final vector of "desk") | 0.5 | -1.0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | |
    | W_vocab column "water" | 0.6 | -0.4 | 0.5 | 0.9 | |
    | Product | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.50 | 1.80 | 3.00 |
    The other 4 columns work the same way:

    |= the |= desk |= water |= cat |= on |
    | -0.70 | 1.25 | 3.00 | 0.50 | -0.15 |
note_053:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>turn the logits into probabilities</back>
    that sum to 1.
    probability = <back:yellow>e^logit / (sum of all e^logit)</back>:
    <back:yellow>a bigger logit gets a bigger share, and every</back>
    share is positive.
    **Toy** (T = 1, K = 3; a word cut by Top-K has logit
    -inf, and e^-inf = 0):

    |= Word |= Logit |= e^logit |= Probability |
    | water | 3.00 | 20.086 | 0.796 |
    | desk | 1.25 | 3.490 | 0.138 |
    | cat | 0.50 | 1.649 | 0.065 |
    | on | -inf | 0 | 0 |
    | the | -inf | 0 | 0 |
    | Sum | | 25.225 | 1.00 |
note_054:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>pick the next token.</back>
    <back:yellow>Top-P</back> keeps the smallest set of likely tokens whose
    probabilities add up to at least P; one is <back:yellow>sampled</back>
    from it. **Why:** <back:yellow>a fixed Top-K cannot adapt.</back> When the
    model is sure it still keeps K words; when it is
    unsure it cuts good ones. <back:yellow>The Top-P set grows or</back>
    <back:yellow>shrinks with the model's confidence.</back>
    **Toy** (T = 1, K = 3, P = 0.9): after Top-K and Softmax:

    |= Word |= Probability |= Running total |= Kept? |
    | water | 0.796 | 0.80 | yes |
    | desk | 0.138 | 0.93 (at least 0.9: stop) | yes |
    | cat | 0.065 | | no |
    Sample from water and desk (renormalized): water 85%,
    desk 15%. A random number in [0, 1) decides: below
    0.85 -> water, otherwise desk. So the same prompt can
    <back:yellow>give different words.</back> T = 0 skips sampling and takes
    the top word. A fixed random seed repeats the draws.
note_055:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>keep only the last position's vector,</back>
    the one that predicts the next token.
    While generating; training keeps every position.
note_056:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>shape the choice before the probabilities.</back>
    <back:yellow>Temperature T</back>: every logit is divided by T before
    Softmax. T < 1 stretches the gaps (the top word gets
    more probability, safer); T > 1 shrinks them (other
    words get a chance, more varied).
    Toy logits after dividing by T (all 5 words, no Top-K):

    |= T |= the |= desk |= water |= cat |= on |= chance of water |
    | 1 (unchanged) | -0.70 | 1.25 | 3.00 | 0.50 | -0.15 | 76% |
    | 0.5 (x 2) | -1.40 | 2.50 | 6.00 | 1.00 | -0.30 | 96% |
    | 2 (/ 2) | -0.35 | 0.625 | 1.50 | 0.25 | -0.075 | 48% |
    <back:yellow>Top-K</back>: keeps only the K highest logits (K = 3: water,
    desk, cat); the others can never be picked.
note_057:
**Purpose:** <back:yellow>close the loop.</back>
    The token is <back:yellow>appended</back> to the input and the whole
    flow repeats from the top, until an <back:yellow>EOS token</back>
    or the max length.
note_059:
Orange arrows = <back:yellow>residual connections</back> (skip paths).
    The block input X (one row per token) is copied:
    ""X  (block input, one row per token)""
    ""├─ copy 1 ─► RMSNorm ─► Attention ─► A ─┐""
    ""└─ copy 2 ─ skip ───────────────────────┴─► X1 = X + A""
    One copy goes through attention; the other skips around
    it. They are then added, row by row: X + A (A = attention's
    result). The same again around the FFN.
    <back:yellow>Both sides must have the same shape</back>, or the add is not possible.
note_058:
**Applied to the logits that remain, after Temperature and Top-K:**
* **Softmax:** probability = e^logit / (sum of all e^logit). <back:yellow>A bigger logit gets a bigger share; all shares sum to 1.</back>
|= T = 1, K = 3 |= water |= desk |= cat |= on, the (cut) |= Sum |
| Logit | 3.00 | 1.25 | 0.50 | -inf | |
| e^logit | 20.086 | 3.490 | 1.649 | 0 (e^-inf) | 25.225 |
| Probability | 0.796 | 0.138 | 0.065 | 0 | 1.00 |
note_060:
**Glossary** (sizes used in this diagram)
    |= Name |= Meaning |= Kind |= Toy |= Llama 3 8B |
    | d_model | length of one token's vector (the model's "width") | chosen by the designers | 4 | 4096 |
    | n_heads | number of attention heads running in parallel | chosen by the designers | 2 | 32 |
    | d_head | numbers per head in Q, K, V = d_model / n_heads | calculated | 2 | 128 |
    | d_k | length of one Key (or Query) vector = d_head; scores are divided by sqrt(d_k) | calculated | 2 | 128 |
    | Q, K, V | what a token looks for, what it offers, what it passes on (per head) | computed from the input | 2 numbers per token | 128 per token |
    | W_Q, W_K, W_V | matrices with d_model rows and d_head columns\n(one set per head). Multiply the input by W_Q\nto get Q, by W_K to get K, by W_V to get V | learned in training | 4 rows, 2 columns | 4096 rows, 128 columns |
    | W_O | matrix with d_model rows and d_model columns (one per block, not per head).\nMultiply the heads joined side by side (n_heads × d_head = d_model numbers)\nby W_O to mix them into the attention output | learned in training | 4 rows, 4 columns | 4096 rows, 4096 columns |
    | gamma | the scale RMSNorm multiplies in after normalizing | learned in training | 4 numbers | 4096 numbers |
    <back:yellow>n_heads × d_head = d_model (toy: 2 × 2 = 4): the heads side by side give back the full width.</back>
note_061:
**Where do W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O come from?**
    <back:yellow>They are not written by hand: they are learned in training.</back>
    **Step 0: choose the sizes** (the designers, before training).
    Toy: d_model = 4, n_heads = 2, so d_head = 4 / 2 = 2.
    Each of W_Q, W_K, W_V then has d_model rows and d_head
    columns: 4 rows and 2 columns = 8 numbers. W_O has d_model
    rows and d_model columns: 4 rows, 4 columns = 16 numbers.
    **Step 1: start random.** Every number is a small random
    value. W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O each get their own.
    **Step 2: train.** The model guesses the next word on lots of
    text; its error nudges every number a tiny bit (backward pass,
    optimizer AdamW), billions of times. For W_Q in the toy:
    ""        start (random)        trained""
    "" 0.12 -0.31    ->    -0.50  0.00""
    ""-0.07  0.25    ->    -0.25 -0.25""
    "" 0.30  0.05    ->    -0.75  0.50""
    ""-0.22  0.18    ->    -0.25 -1.00""
    **Step 3: freeze.** <back:yellow>When generating, the weights no longer change: only the input does.</back>
    Every block, and every head in it, has its own W_Q, W_K, W_V.
    Every block has its own W_O (one per block, not per head).
    (The toy numbers are assumed.)
note_062:
**Where does gamma come from?**
    <back:yellow>Like W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O, it is not written by hand: it is learned in training.</back>
    **Step 0: choose the size.** gamma has one number per
    position of the token vector: d_model = 4 numbers in the
    toy (4096 in Llama 3 8B).
    **Step 1: start at 1.** Usually all ones, so at the start
    RMSNorm only rescales and gamma changes nothing.
    **Step 2: train.** The same loop as W_Q: the model guesses the
    next word, and its error nudges each gamma number a tiny bit,
    billions of times. For gamma in the toy:
    ""start     [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]""
    ""trained   [0.9, 1.3, 0.7, 1.1]""
    Applied to the normalized vector from above (multiply
    each position by its own gamma):
    ""normalized   [0.2,  1.0, 1.0, 1.4]""
    ""gamma        [0.9,  1.3, 0.7, 1.1]  (trained)""
    ""output       [0.18, 1.3, 0.7, 1.54]""
    **Step 3: freeze.** <back:yellow>When generating, gamma no longer changes: the same gamma is used for every token.</back>
    Every RMSNorm (before attention and before the FFN in each
    block, and the final one) has its own gamma.
    (The trained numbers here are assumed.)
